title: An Ancient Ocean of Giant Predators Changes Ideas About Evolution
summary: Long ago, an ocean covered what is now central Colombia, and giant sea reptiles ruled the waves. Long-necked plesiosaurs swam beside sea crocodiles, turtles, sharks and crustaceans. Now fossils from that lost world are changing how scientists think about evolution. Scientists from McGill University and Colombia studied fossils from the Paja Formation, near Villa de Leyva. The rocks, from the Early Cretaceous period, preserve a picture of an ocean community called the Paja Biota. Ancient animal groups from the Jurassic period, already heading toward extinction, lived side by side with newer Cretaceous groups just beginning to flourish. The food web was also very intricate, with an unusually large variety of top predators. Hans Larsson and Dirley Cortés call this pattern a 'Biotic Inflection,' when older groups nearing extinction live alongside newer ones starting to expand. The scientists think a 'perfect storm' made it possible: warm temperatures, high sea levels and nutrient-rich waters. The big idea is that major changes in life on Earth do not always need a mass extinction. But more evidence is needed: more fossils and better dates.
why_it_matters: If you love dinosaurs or sea creatures, this story shows how fossils can change what scientists think about life long ago.
